abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework that reconceptualizes implicit neural representations through differential geometry, fundamentally changing how we understand and design neural networks for visual media computation. Unlike conventional approaches that treat such representations as black-box function approximators, our framework characterizes continuous signals as embedded manifolds in high-dimensional spaces. This geometric perspective reveals fundamental relationships between network architecture, activation functions, and the topological properties of represented signals. We introduce the concept of spectral curvature continuity, which provides a principled way to analyze and control the smoothness of learned representations. Based on this theory, we derive architectural constraints that guarantee desirable geometric properties, leading to a new class of networks termed Geometric Implicit Networks. Our analysis demonstrates that these networks exhibit superior convergence properties and frequency control compared to existing methods. Extensive experiments on 3D modeling, scene reconstruction, and computational photography tasks validate the theoretical findings and show remarkable improvements in representation accuracy and generalization. This work establishes a new paradigm for understanding neural representations in computer graphics and visual computing, opening promising research directions for geometric deep learning.

This paper develops a rigorous theoretical foundation based on optimal transport theory to address fundamental limitations in adaptive sampling strategies for photorealistic rendering. Existing adaptive sampling methods typically rely on heuristic variance estimators, lacking theoretical guarantees for convergence and optimality. Our approach reformulates the sampling problem as an optimal transport problem, where the goal is to find the optimal sample distribution that minimizes the earth mover's distance between sampling and target light transport functions. We derive a closed-form solution for importance sampling in bounded domains and present an efficient iterative algorithm for unconstrained domains. The optimal transport framework provides a unified treatment of various rendering phenomena including glossy reflections, volumetric scattering, and participating media, revealing deep connections between previously disparate techniques. Our analysis proves that transport-based sampling achieves lower sample complexity than conventional variance-based methods. Experimental results on complex scenes demonstrate significant improvements in convergence rates, with reductions in mean squared error of up to 40% compared to state-of-the-art adaptive sampling techniques while maintaining theoretical optimality guarantees.

We present ShaderFlow, a novel dataflow architecture that fundamentally reimagines the computational pipeline for real-time neural rendering in visual media. Unlike traditional GPU-based rendering systems that follow imperative programming models, ShaderFlow represents rendering operations as a directed graph of composable neural modules. This architectural paradigm enables automatic optimization of the rendering pipeline through graph-level optimization, automatic differentiation through arbitrary shading operations, and seamless integration of physically-based and neural rendering techniques. The system introduces adaptive module composition, which dynamically adjusts the computational graph based on scene complexity and available computational resources. We implement a complete neural rendering pipeline supporting real-time image synthesis, dynamic lighting, and interactive material editing. Benchmarks on standard computer graphics benchmarks demonstrate that ShaderFlow achieves comparable quality to state-of-the-art neural rendering methods while maintaining interactive frame rates on consumer hardware. The dataflow architecture enables novel applications including procedural neural materials, real-time neural texture synthesis, and interactive visual debugging of rendering operations, representing a paradigm shift in rendering system design.

We present a complete system for multi-resolution urban reconstruction enabling scalable visual analytics of city-scale environments. The system integrates recent advances in multi-view stereo reconstruction, mesh simplification, and texture optimization into a unified pipeline optimized for visual analytics workflows. We introduce adaptive level-of-detail generation producing hierarchical mesh representations with consistent topology, enabling seamless transitions between detail levels during interactive exploration. The pipeline includes novel texture atlasing that preserves semantic coherence across resolution levels, supporting consistent material editing and annotation. Our memory management system enables streaming urban-scale scenes with millions of buildings on commodity hardware through efficient spatial indexing for real-time visibility culling and spatial queries essential for urban visual analytics. Evaluation on datasets spanning multiple cities demonstrates order-of-magnitude improvements in reconstruction speed compared to existing workflows, with negligible loss in visual quality. The system has been deployed in production for urban planning, cultural heritage documentation, and autonomous vehicle simulation, representing significant practical advancement in large-scale geometric computing and visual analytics infrastructure.
